ending.why: Judged against 001-pilot, the only aired episode, from the second hook to the end. Everything round 1 blocked is gone, and nothing has been put in its place that the show has done. The aired song ended on lights down, the host alone and unsure, a flat spoken line that folded him in, and a full-band chorus with its person changed so that everyone was inside it. Here the lights do not change, the music does not stop, nobody speaks inside the song, nobody is singled out, the host does not sing, nothing is sung at the lens, and the hook's words are the same every time. What changes at the end is the genre's own: a lift of a whole step and one more 'doo-wop'. The aired song had no key change, no third verse and no closing picture of this kind. The feeling at the end is no longer a place being made for someone; it is a small thing being taken up (three words by the week), which is the song's own subject and not the aired one. Weighed and not counted: (1) Themed weeks are a subject the aired monologue used, for a joke about two weeks falling on one day. Here the surprise is who named the week and how little it took. The subject returns with a different turn, and nothing points back. (2) A real post on a card at the song's warmest moment: the aired close built its sincere beat from real posts held on cards as the answer to a question asked all night. Here there is no question; the card is the last item of a list, it is three words, and it lights on the sung count. A post card is a primitive and it does a different job. (3) The camera's travel back along the row ends on the band's own two cards, so the show's entry is again the last thing on a list of members' things. In the aired song that was a reveal that the wished-for thing was the song itself, with the host pinned inside it. Here it is the bottom of a shrinking list, two syllables after three words, with nobody inside anything. I passed this picture before the bridge in round 1 and pass it here. (4) Two of the five tiles the last traverse passes are this episode's own earlier segments. It is the song going back over its own row and not the night, so it is not the aired habit of a song recapping the episode, but it is the nearest this draft comes to it, and the final review should look again if the song is moved to the last place. (5) The button, the host taking the applause in the song's own verb and two band members answering with their syllables, is a host's button and the band's last word, which are the format's bones; the joke is new.

message: Yes, and more wholly than before: the ending now stands on a third thing from the window, three words from a small account that became what the week was called, so the song shows one thing three times at shrinking sizes (a simulator, a mug, three words, with the band's two syllables next in line), no line states it, and no part of it could now be sung in another week; what went with the host is the back half's one warm laugh, not its meaning.
inside: The three words answer the coffee segment, where a member's puppet says 'polyhedron week comes in many forms' and nothing in the episode has said what that week is: a true callback, and it gives the episode its frame, but the card's handle is nearly the same as the small account's on the coffee segment's hero card, and with the two segments side by side a viewer will take two people for one, which the screening ruling on those two accounts is there to prevent. The long camera move back past every item in order, ending on the show's own small part, is also how the making-of leaves three segments earlier, and the button is still the third in the episode on the host alone and dry about himself, though the song itself no longer turns on him.
airWhy: I would air the alternative, with a segment between it and the coffee segment: its ending is now its own, it is the week's from first line to last where the present song is one maker's cat for the second time, and it brings in a new small account and tells the episode what week it is, at the cost of a back half that is warm and no longer funny (funny down one with the host's note gone, variety up one).
